sections.report:
**Section.** The whole piece: applies.

**Findings**
1. **Do the main image and the headline make one idea together, with neither just repeating the other? No.** The illustration (x 120–460, y 150–493) is a generic lighthouse: red cap, yellow lantern, one red band, flat sea. The headline "The light at Gull Point" (x 508–936, y 145–185) already tells you this is a lighthouse, so the picture only says it again. Nothing in the picture belongs to *this* place. The copy names things you could draw: the estuary mouth, the ninety steps, the gallery view, the ferry crossing to the harbour wall, the tea-room cottage. The picture shows none of them, so it could sit on any lighthouse page and gives the visitor no reason to pick this one. The catalog's only source for this rule (Bernbach/DDB) is off the approved list, so I'm arguing it on its own merits. This is an editorial or visitor page, not an ad, and a picture of the subject is a normal pairing, which is why the weight is low. Fix: keep the flat style but make the picture show what the copy promises, such as the view from the gallery with the ferry crossing the bay, or the tower on its point with the cottage beside it. Then the picture adds the reason to visit and the headline names the place. Taste. Weight: minor.

**What's working.**
- The type, colours and shapes share one mood. The warm, bookish serif, the soft blues, and the flat red/yellow/cream shapes all feel gentle, coastal and a little old-fashioned. That suits a heritage tower with scones in the tea room, and nothing feels out of place.
- The copy is finished and reads like a person talking. It moves from history ("keepers… remembered by the brass plaques") to now ("open to visitors on summer weekends") to the practical next step ("Tickets are sold at the cottage by the car park"), so a first-time reader knows what the place is and how to visit.

**Checklist.** The whole piece: 8 lines, 7 yes, 1 no (image and headline make one idea)

**Walk (working notes)**

First read: the eye goes to the lighthouse illustration first, because the red roof and band stand out against the pale sky. It then moves right to the bold headline "The light at Gull Point" and down into three short paragraphs. It reads as a short visitor-information feature about a lighthouse, aimed at day-trippers. It feels calm and plain.

Job (assumed): a web page or section that introduces a lighthouse and tells visitors they can climb it and where to buy tickets.

What matters first:
- One element dominates by size or contrast: **yes**. The illustration (about 120–460 x, 150–493 y) and the headline work as a pair. The picture catches the eye and the headline names it, so there is a clear place to start.
- Text levels distinct, no near-same sizes: **yes**. There are two levels. The headline looks about 2× the body size, and nothing sits in between.
- Headings differ by more than size: **yes**. The headline is bold and dark, and the body is regular weight in the same serif.

No line was answered no or unsure, so I opened no entries.

---

**Section.** What matters first (hierarchy): applies.

**Findings**
None.

**What's working.**
- **Picture and headline lead together.** The illustration's saturated red and yellow pull the eye in first. The heavy headline sits level with the top of the picture (headline about y 145–185, picture top at y 150), so the eye goes straight from the image to its name. Keep the headline's top aligned with the picture's top.
- **Two text levels with a big step between them.** The headline is bold at roughly twice the body size. The three paragraphs share one size and weight, with no subheads or in-between sizes to blur the order. For text this short, two levels are enough, and the big gap makes the order clear at a glance.

**Checklist.** What matters first: 3 lines, 3 yes, 0 no, 0 unsure

**Section.** Arrangement and space: applies.

**Findings**
1. **Is every element either exactly aligned with an edge or axis it shares with another, or clearly off it, with no near-misses of a few pixels?** The top of the picture is at about y 150. The tops of the heading's capitals and ascenders ("T", "h", "l", "G", "P") look to be at about y 143–148, so the heading rises a few pixels above the picture. At the bottom the two columns do line up: the baseline of "it bakes scones every morning." sits at about y 493, on the picture's bottom edge. With the bottom exact and the top nearly exact, the pair looks meant to line up but slightly off at the head. Most viewers won't notice, but it is the kind of small miss that makes a layout look a touch unfinished (Arnheim, *Art and Visual Perception*, ch. I "Balance": a placement that is neither clearly here nor clearly there makes the eye waver). Müller-Brockmann's "pictures fit the grid" asks for exactly this pairing: the picture's top on the first line of text and its bottom on the last. Fix: measure it, then set the picture's top on the heading's cap height, or on the first body line if that is the intended reference, so the top is as exact as the bottom. I couldn't crop (Bash was denied), so this comes from the full image and needs a pixel check. Convention. Weight: minor.

**What's working.**
- The space is gathered, not scattered. Picture and text form one tight unit with a single 48 px gutter (x 460 to 508). The open space is two large bands, about 150 px above the unit and about 300 px below it, plus a 120–140 px side margin. The eye gets one clear thing to look at and plenty of room around it (Ruder, *Typography*, "Contrasts").
- The grouping by space is clear and correctly ordered. The heading sits close to the first paragraph. The three paragraphs are separated by a gap only a little larger than their line spacing. The gutter between picture and text is clearly wider than any of those. The heading, picture and story read as one item without a box or rule (Arnheim, ch. II, proximity). The picture-to-text ratio of about 1:2 gives a calm, deliberate split.

**Couldn't judge from a still.** The bottom alignment works only because of this copy's length. With longer or shorter text, or a narrower window where the text column reflows, the last line won't land on the picture's bottom edge. Check whether the alignment is built in or a coincidence.

**Checklist.** Arrangement and space: 13 lines, 12 yes, 1 no (exactly aligned or clearly off, no near-misses)

sections.report:
**Section.** Text: applies.

**Findings**
1. *Do paragraphs and columns break cleanly, with no lone short word on a last line and no heading at the foot of a column?* No. The first paragraph ends with "room." alone on its last line (about x 508–562, y 297–317). Three full lines are followed by one five-character word. The paragraph's shape breaks, a large white gap opens before paragraph 2, and the word reads as an afterthought. The phrase it belongs to, "the lamp room", is also split across the line break. Bringhurst, *The Elements of Typographic Style* §2.4.2, says a paragraph should not end with one short word alone on its last line. Fix: pull "lamp room." onto the last line together. Use a non-breaking space between "lamp" and "room", or `text-wrap: pretty`, or trim a word from the sentence. Convention. Minor.

**What's working.**
- The body text is easy to read. It's a plain text serif at a comfortable size, dark on white, with lines of about 60 to 70 characters and generous leading. A visitor reads the three short paragraphs without effort.
- The type plan holds together. One serif family does all the work: a bold cut for the one-line heading and the regular cut for the body. Spacing alone separates the paragraphs. Nothing competes with anything else and there's no stray face.

**Checklist.** Text: 30 lines, 29 yes, 1 no (paragraphs break cleanly).

I found one problem in the Color section, and it's minor. The colour on this page is restrained and works well. The one weakness is that the white lighthouse tower is about as light as the pale sky behind it, so the outline of the picture's main subject relies on hue alone.

**Section.** Color: applies.

**Findings**
1. **Does the piece hold a clear range of light and dark, so its structure still shows in grayscale? No.**
   - **Where:** In the illustration (x 120–460, y 150–492), the cream tower (about x 258–322, y 241–396) stands on a pale blue sky. The two look almost equally light. By eye, the contrast between them is only about 1.1–1.2:1.
   - **What the viewer experiences:** In colour, the warm cream against the cool blue just about separates the tower. In grayscale, in print, on a washed-out screen or in bright light, the tower's outline mostly disappears. What remains is a red band and a red roof floating over the sea. The tower is the subject of the picture and of the headline, and its shape is the weakest edge in the image. Elsewhere the value structure is good: the dark sea against the light sky, and the black text on white.
   - **Why:** Figure and ground should survive a grayscale render. When hue alone separates two shapes, the pairing is fragile (Albers, *Interaction of Color*; Wathan and Schoger, *Refactoring UI*, "Don't rely on color alone").
   - **Fix:** Give the tower a clear step in lightness from the sky. Either darken the sky to a mid blue so the cream tower reads as the lightest shape, or add a thin darker outline or shaded side to the tower. Keep the warm-against-cool scheme. Check the result by viewing the illustration in grayscale.
   - **Kind:** Convention. **Weight:** Minor. The picture is decorative next to the article, and the red band, the roof and the sea still say "lighthouse".

**What's working.**
- **Restraint.** The page is white with near-black text, and all the colour sits inside the one illustration. The picture is the only colourful thing, so it carries the mood (seaside, sunny, friendly) without competing with the headline or the body text.
- **Warm against cool.** The red, yellow and cream of the tower sit on cool blues, so the lighthouse comes forward and the sky and sea recede. The red appears only twice, on the roof and the band, so it stays an accent that suits a lighthouse rather than spreading across the picture.

**Checklist.** Color: 9 lines, 8 yes, 1 no (clear range of light and dark).

**Section.** Pictures: applies. There is one flat vector illustration of a lighthouse at x 120–460, y 150–493.

**Findings**
1. **Does each crop look intended, with no limb cut at a joint and no edges that just touch?** The tower's flat base meets the horizon at exactly y≈395 (x≈258–322). There is no rock, headland or shoreline under it. The picture reads as a cutout set on the waterline, so the lighthouse looks like it's floating on open sea rather than standing on a point. That undercuts the "Gull Point" in the headline and the "mouth of the estuary" in the copy. The reason is common sense; the catalog entry's sources aren't on the approved list. When a shape's edge just touches another, the eye can't tell whether the two are joined or merely stacked. To fix it, set the base clearly into something: a rock or headland shape that overlaps the waterline, or sink the base slightly behind the front wave so the tower is planted. Mark: taste. Weight: minor. The picture still says "lighthouse by the sea" instantly, and fixing this would make it more convincing without changing how well the page works.

**What's working.**
- The illustration is crisp, flat and consistent throughout. It has no strokes, gradients or fake lighting, and the shapes are simple and geometric, all at one level of detail. That gives it a clean, editorial calm that suits the quiet serif text beside it.
- The tower picks itself out without help. The cream body sits close in value to the pale sky, but the red band, red roof and yellow lantern make it the clear subject, and they're the only warm colours on the page. That pulls the eye to the picture first and ties it to the subject of the headline.

**Checklist.** Pictures: 12 lines, 11 yes, 1 no (crop looks intended, no edges that just touch)

**Section.** Charts and data: skipped. The page has no chart, table of figures or dashboard, only a flat lighthouse illustration and body text.

**Findings**
None.

**Checklist.** Charts and data: skipped
